# Emissary Docs (full text)

> The prose documentation for Emissary, a platform for LLM model routing, post-training and inference. See https://docs.withemissary.com/llms.txt for the index.


---

# Emissary docs: LLM routing, post-training, inference

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com

# Emissary documentation

**Emissary** is a platform for **LLM model routing, post-training and inference**. Route each request
to the model best suited to handle it, post-train models of your own on your data, and serve base and
fine-tuned models on managed GPU infrastructure. Emissary replaces slow, expensive frontier-model
calls with small, purpose-built classifiers that return the same decision in milliseconds for a
fraction of the cost, with no prompt engineering and no full-size model in the loop.

## What can I do with Emissary?

### Model routing

Send each request to the cheapest model that can do the job, behind one OpenAI- and
Anthropic-compatible gateway URL. Typical savings are 30–50%.

[What is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing) · [Get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started) ·
[Reduce LLM costs](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/reduce-llm-costs)

### Post-training

Adapt a base model to your task with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning
(GRPO), then compare checkpoints and deploy the best one.

[What is post-training?](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/what-is-post-training) ·
[Quickstart](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/quickstart) · [Datasets](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/datasets)

### Inference

Serve base models and fine-tuned LoRA adapters on managed GPUs, with autoscaling from a single
instance to a cluster of replicas.

[What is LLM inference?](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/what-is-llm-inference) ·
[Deployments](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/deployments) · [Autoscaling](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/autoscaling)

## Quickstart

The fastest way to get started is one of our quick start guides. Each walks you through building
your first model three ways: the public playground (no signup), the dashboard UI, and the API.

- **[Create Your First Judge](https://docs.withemissary.com/quickstart/llm-as-judge)**: score any text against criteria you
  define (for example *helpfulness* or *factual accuracy*) and get back a calibrated probability
  instead of a vague verdict.
- **[Create Your First ModelRouter](https://docs.withemissary.com/quickstart/router)**: automatically send each query to the
  model best suited to handle it, so you stop hard-coding one model for every request.

Want a router that also accounts for cache state, effort and output length? Start with
[model routing: get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started). Want to train your own models? See the
[post-training quickstart](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/quickstart).

## How do the pieces fit together?

Routing, post-training and inference form a loop. Every routed request leaves a trajectory, so you
learn which requests are easy and which no model can handle. You serve the open models you rely on
from dedicated capacity, and you post-train models of your own on that traffic. The router sends work
to them when they're the better call, which makes routing cheaper again. See
[what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).

## Reference

- [API reference](https://docs.withemissary.com/api): REST endpoints for projects, datasets, training jobs, engines and
  deployments.
- [Glossary](https://docs.withemissary.com/glossary): definitions of the terms used across these docs.
- [llms.txt](https://docs.withemissary.com/llms.txt): a plain-text index of these docs for LLMs and
  AI assistants.


---

# LLM routing, post-training and inference glossary

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/glossary

Short definitions of the terms used across the Emissary docs, grouped by topic. Each links to the
page that explains it in full.

## Model routing

### Model routing

Choosing, for each request, which model should handle it. See [what is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing).

### Model router (also LLM router)

Software that sits in front of a pool of models, reads each request, and sends it to the model best suited to it. See [routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways).

### Gateway (also LLM gateway)

Infrastructure for how requests reach models: one interface over many providers, with credentials, retries, rate limits, load balancing and failover. A gateway doesn't decide which model is right. See [routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways).

### Catalog

The set of models a router can route across. See [choose your models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models).

### Default model

The anchor of a router's policy. It serves any request that no model is confident about, so choose one you'd trust with any request.

### Confidence

The router's estimate of the probability that a given model completes a request. There is one estimate per model and effort level. See [how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

### Confidence threshold

How confident the router must be that a model can complete a request before that model may serve it. The default is 0.80. A higher threshold is more conservative, and a lower one saves more. See [set the confidence threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold).

### Confident pool

The models in your catalog whose confidence clears the threshold for a given request. The cheapest of them serves the request.

### Routing reason

The recorded explanation of why a request went to a model, such as `cheapest_confident` or `default_no_confident`. See [monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).

### Escalation

When the default model isn't confident but a more expensive model is, and the request is sent to the more expensive one.

### Deflection

A request served by a model other than the default model.

### Performance-based routing

Routing that asks which models can actually do the task, based on how they have performed. Compare **complexity-based routing**, which guesses how hard a task is from its input. See [the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space).

### Stateful routing

Routing that tracks the current situation, most importantly cache state, rather than deciding each request in isolation. See [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#cache-state).

### Prompt cache

Context a model has already processed and holds, which makes sending the same conversation back to it cheaper. Switching models forfeits the previous model's cache.

### Effort

How much reasoning a model applies to a request, which trades more reasoning for more cost and latency. The router can change effort instead of switching models, which keeps the cache. See [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#effort).

### Intelligence density

How many output tokens a model needs to complete a task. A router that is intelligence-density aware prices that in rather than comparing per-token prices alone.

### Zero data retention

A router setting, on by default, under which Emissary doesn't retain input, output or session replay data from gateway traffic. See [get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started).

## Post-training

### Post-training

Adapting a base model to your task by changing its weights, rather than only changing its input as prompting does. See [what is post-training?](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/what-is-post-training).

### Fine-tuning

Training a model on examples of your task. Often used interchangeably with post-training.

### SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning)

A technique that trains the model to reproduce the input-to-output pairs in your dataset. See [concepts](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/concept#post-training-techniques).

### GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)

A reinforcement-learning technique that improves the model against a reward signal by comparing several sampled completions per prompt. Available for the `text-generation` task type.

### LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapter

A small set of weight layers added on top of a frozen base model instead of rewriting all of its weights. Fine-tunes on Emissary are LoRA adapters, so many can share one base model.

### Base model

The foundation model you adapt: either a published pre-trained model, or one of your own existing checkpoints.

### Task type

What your model does, such as `text-generation`, `classification`, `regression`, `embedding` or `ner`. It determines the dataset schema, the model's output and the API you call.

### Training project

A workspace that groups the training jobs you run toward a single goal.

### Training job

One post-training run, tying together a base model, a technique, your data and your hyperparameters.

### Checkpoint

A snapshot of the model captured during training, typically one per epoch. Each is independently evaluable and deployable.

### Hyperparameters

The settings of a training run, such as learning rate and number of epochs. See [hyperparameters](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/parameters).

### Test function

A metric function that takes the input, the expected output and the predicted output, and returns a numeric score for a checkpoint.

### Overfitting

When a model fits its training data so closely that it performs worse on data it hasn't seen. It's why a later checkpoint isn't always better.

## Inference

### Inference

Running a trained model on new input to produce an output. See [what is LLM inference?](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/what-is-llm-inference).

### Inference engine

A managed, GPU-backed serving unit, bound to one base model and one task type. See [concepts](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/concept).

### Deployment

A specific model version served on an engine, called by name. Either a **base model deployment** or a **fine-tuned deployment**. See [deployments](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/deployments).

### Replica

One GPU-backed copy of an engine, handling a share of its traffic. See [autoscaling](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/autoscaling).

### Autoscaling

Adding replicas when load rises and removing them when it falls, between a minimum and a maximum you set.

### On-demand engine

An engine on a single GPU instance with fixed capacity. The default server type.

### Cluster engine

A horizontally scalable, multi-replica engine, used automatically when you enable autoscaling.


---

# ModelRouter quickstart: your first LLM router

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/quickstart/router

Looking for the stateful model router that also accounts for cache state, effort and output length?
See [model routing: get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started). This quickstart creates the classifier-based
router described below.

A **model router** automatically sends each query to the model best suited to handle it — a small, fast model for simple questions, a heavyweight reasoning model for complex ones — so you don't hard-code one model for every request.

Emissary makes that routing decision with a small, purpose-built classifier rather than a full frontier model. It picks the right route in about **56 ms** at **$0.23 per 10k requests**, versus the **1.5–4.7 seconds** and **$5–7 per 10k requests** a frontier model takes to make the same call (see the side-by-side comparison in Path A). And because each query goes to the right-sized model, you avoid paying top-tier prices on requests a smaller model handles just as well.

You can create your first router three ways. Pick whichever fits:

- **[Path A — Public Playground (no signup)](#path-a--public-playground-no-signup):** the fastest way to see it work.
- **[Path B — Dashboard (UI)](#path-b--dashboard-ui):** build and save a router from your dashboard.
- **[Path C — Dashboard (API)](#path-c--dashboard-api):** create the same router programmatically.

All three share the same building block, defined once below.

---

## Core concept: Routes

A router is defined by its **routes** — the set of destinations a query can be sent to. Each route has two fields:

- **Name** — a short identifier for the destination (e.g., `simple_task`, `Claude Opus`, `GPT 5`). It's the label that appears in your results, so keep it concise.
- **Description** — what kind of query should go to this route. Be specific; this is what the router matches an incoming query against (e.g., *"Complex queries requiring reasoning, code generation, or multi-step analysis."*).

For each query, the router returns a **probability per route**, and the route with the highest probability is the one to send the query to. Every path below is just a different way to define these routes.

---

## Path A — Public Playground (no signup)

Open the [public playground](https://www.withemissary.com/demo?mode=routing). You'll land on a ready-to-use router with our default configuration: a simple `task` router that sorts a query by complexity into `simple_task`, `complex_task`, or `creative_task`. Type any input and hit **Run** — no sign-in required.

You'll get the router's decision alongside the same input run through frontier models (Claude, GPT), so you can compare result, latency, and cost side by side. In this example the Tower-of-Hanoi task is classified as **`complex_task` (93.4%)**, and all three models agree on `complex_task` — but Emissary returns that decision in ~56 ms for $0.23 / 10k requests, versus seconds and dollars for the frontier models.

### Customize your router

The default `task` router only labels complexity. To make it route to actual models, edit the list of routes in the left sidebar. For example, to route between three models:

| # | Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `Claude Haiku` | Simple, straightforward queries that can be handled by a small, fast model. |
| 2 | `Claude Opus` | Complex queries requiring reasoning, code generation, or multi-step analysis. |
| 3 | `GPT 5` | Creative writing, brainstorming, or content generation tasks. |

Hit **Save**. That's it — you've built a custom router. Test it with any input to see where it routes.

### Deploy & integrate

When you're ready, hit **Deploy** in the **Ready to integrate?** section to turn your playground router into a live API endpoint. (Sign up / sign in to get your API key.)

Your router is saved as an **Experiment**, and the **Integration** tab gives you a copy-paste snippet with your real model name and key prefilled. See [Integration](#integration) below.

---

## Path B — Dashboard (UI)

From the **Playground** tab, click **New experiment**.

### 1. Identity & mode

- **Name** — how you'll recognize this experiment in the Playground list (e.g., `ModelRouter`).
- **Mode** — select **Model Router**.

### 2. Router config

Define each route's **Name** and **Description** ([defined above](#customize-your-router)). We'll use the same three routes as in Path A. Add more by clicking **Add route** at the top right.

Click **Create & run zero-shot**

### Test it

From the Playground tab, type any input ("Design and implement a infrastructure platform") and hit **Run** to see your router's decision next to the frontier models.

Ready to ship it? Head to [Integration](#integration).

---

## Path C — Dashboard (API)

Prefer code? Create the same `ModelRouter` programmatically. You can create an API key under **Settings → Credentials**.

**1. Create the experiment**

```python

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments",
    headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-API-Key": YOUR_API_KEY,
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'ModelRouter',
        'mode': 'routing',
        'classes': [
            {'name': 'Claude Haiku',   'description': 'Simple, straightforward queries that can be handled by a small, fast model.'},
            {'name': 'Claude Opus',  'description': 'Complex queries requiring reasoning, code generation, or multi-step analysis.'},
            {'name': 'GPT 5', 'description': 'Creative writing, brainstorming, or content generation tasks.'}
        ]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

```json
{ "id": "ex-ahejacuehandheha", "latest_version": "0.0.0" }
```

**2. Call the router**

```python
response = requests.post(
    "https://api.withemissary.com/v1/classification",
    headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-API-Key": YOUR_API_KEY,
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        "model": "ex-ahejacuehandheha/0.0.0",  # <experiment_id>/<version>
        "input": "Design and implement a infrastructure platform",
        "data_format": "probs",
    }),
)
print(response.json())
```

```json
{
    "id": "classify-fec5cbf726b44af2ade51065232ad182",
    "model": "ex-ahejacuehandheha/0.0.0",
    "data": [{
            "index": 0,
            "probs": {
                    "Claude Haiku": 0.09003042429685593,
                    "Claude Opus": 0.8626418709754944,
                    "GPT 5": 0.047327760607004166
            }
    }],
    "created": 1780085360
}
```

`Claude Opus` has the highest probability (~0.86), so the router would send this query to Claude Opus.

---

## Integration

However you built your router — Path A, B, or C — the **Integration** tab gives you a ready-to-use snippet.

- Switch between **cURL / Python / TypeScript**.
- Your `<experiment_id>/<version>` and **API key are prefilled**.
- Copy it with one click and drop it into your app — the endpoint serves traffic immediately.

**cURL example**

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.withemissary.com/v1/classification" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: <YOUR_API_KEY>" \
  -d '{
    "model": "<experiment_id>/<version>",
    "input": "Design and implement a infrastructure platform",
    "data_format": "probs"
  }'
```

**Response**

```json
{
    "id": "classify-fec5cbf726b44af2ade51065232ad182",
    "model": "ex-ahejacuehandheha/0.0.0",
    "data": [{
            "index": 0,
            "probs": {
                    "Claude Haiku": 0.09003042429685593,
                    "Claude Opus": 0.8626418709754944,
                    "GPT 5": 0.047327760607004166
            }
    }],
    "created": 1780085360
}
```

That's it — your router is live wherever you need it.


---

# LLM-as-a-judge quickstart: create your first judge

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/quickstart/llm-as-judge

**LLM-as-a-judge** (also written LLM as Judge) lets you score any text — a model's answer, a support reply, a user message — against criteria you define, and get back a calibrated probability instead of a vague verdict.

Emissary runs these judges as small, purpose-built classifiers rather than full frontier models. The result: a judgment that takes a frontier model **1.6–2.6 seconds** and **$10–15 per 10k requests** returns on Emissary in about **56 ms** at **$0.29 per 10k requests** — the same verdict, orders of magnitude faster and cheaper (see the side-by-side comparison in Path A).

You can create your first judge three ways. Pick whichever fits:

- **[Path A — Public Playground (no signup)](#path-a--public-playground-no-signup):** the fastest way to see it work.
- **[Path B — Dashboard (UI)](#path-b--dashboard-ui):** build and save a judge from your dashboard.
- **[Path C — Dashboard (API)](#path-c--dashboard-api):** create the same judge programmatically.

All three share the same two building blocks, defined once below.

---

## Core concepts: Metric & Criteria

Every judge is defined by two fields:

- **Metric** — a short identifier for what you're measuring (e.g., `helpful`, `anger`, `factual_accuracy`). It's the label your result appears under, so keep it concise.
- **Criteria** — the instruction the judge uses to score each input, **phrased as a yes/no question.** Be specific about what a "YES" looks like. It can be one line *("Does the response directly answer the user's question?")* or a detailed rubric *("Label YES if the response is factually correct, cites relevant sources, and avoids speculation; NO for unsupported or hallucinated claims. Is the response factually accurate?")*.

Every path below is just a different way to set these two fields.

---

## Path A — Public Playground (no signup)

Open the [public playground](https://www.withemissary.com/demo?mode=judge). You'll land on a ready-to-use judge with our default configuration: a simple **`helpful`** judge that decides whether an assistant's answer actually helps the user. Type any input and hit **Run** — no sign-in required.

You'll get the judge's verdict alongside the same input run through frontier models (Claude, GPT), so you can compare result, latency, and cost side by side. In this example the dismissive answer scores **0% `helpful`** across all three — but Emissary returns that verdict in ~56 ms for $0.29 / 10k requests, versus seconds and dollars for the frontier models.

### Customize your judge

The default `helpful` judge is intentionally minimal. To make it your own, edit the **Metric** and **Criteria** in the left sidebar. For example, to build a judge that detects anger:

- **Metric:** `anger`
- **Criteria:** A text should be labeled as expressing anger (YES) if it contains explicit or strongly implied hostile emotional state directed at a target (person, group, system, or situation), characterized by emotional agitation and adversarial tone. This includes expressions of irritation, frustration, outrage, resentment, or contempt when they are intensified and accompanied by blame, condemnation, or rejection. Indicators include derogatory language, insults, profanity used in a hostile manner, accusatory phrasing, emotionally charged criticism, dismissive or demeaning statements, emphatic negativity (e.g., “this is unacceptable,” “I’m sick of this,” “what the hell is wrong with this”), or any language implying loss of patience or emotional control. Passive or neutral disagreement, calm critique, or factual negative evaluation without emotional escalation should NOT be labeled as anger. The key requirement is the presence of an emotionally activated, antagonistic stance rather than mere negativity or disagreement. Does this text express anger?

Hit **Save**. That's it — you've built a custom judge. Test it with any input ("I'm so mad!") to see how it scores.

### Deploy & integrate

When you're ready, hit **Deploy** in the **Ready to integrate?** section to turn your playground judge into a live API endpoint. (Sign up / sign in to get your API key.)

Your judge is saved as an **Experiment**, and the **Integration** tab gives you a copy-paste snippet with your real model name and key prefilled. See [Integration](#integration) below.

---

## Path B — Dashboard (UI)

From the **Playground** tab, click **New experiment**.

### 1. Identity & mode

- **Name** — how you'll recognize this experiment in the Playground list (e.g., `AngerJudge`).
- **Mode** — select **LLM as Judge**.

### 2. Judge config

Fill in the **Metric** and **Criteria** ([defined above](#customize-your-judge)). We'll use the same `anger` judge as in Path A.

Click **Create & run zero-shot**.

### Test it

From the Playground tab, type any input ("I'm so mad!") and hit **Run** to see your judge's score next to the frontier models.

Ready to ship it? Head to [Integration](#integration).

---

## Path C — Dashboard (API)

Prefer code? Create the same `AngerJudge` programmatically. You can create an API key under **Settings → Credentials**.

**1. Create the experiment**

```python

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments",
    headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-API-Key": YOUR_API_KEY,
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        "name": "AngerJudge",
        "mode": "judge",
        "classes": [
            {"name": "anger", "description": "Does this text express anger?"}
        ],
    }),
)
print(response.json())
```

```json
{ "id": "ex-ahejacuehandheha", "latest_version": "0.0.0" }
```

**2. Call the judge**

```python
response = requests.post(
    "https://api.withemissary.com/v1/classification",
    headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-API-Key": YOUR_API_KEY,
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        "model": "ex-ahejacuehandheha/0.0.0",  # <experiment_id>/<version>
        "input": "I'm so mad!",
        "data_format": "probs",
    }),
)
print(response.json())
```

```json
{
    "id": "classify-3c52592c7a404f97aa494861a79db220",
    "model": "ex-ahejacuehandheha/0.0.0",
    "data": [{ "index": 0, "probs": { "anger": 0.96 } }],
    "created": 1779906329
}
```

A high `anger` probability confirms the judge correctly flagged the angry message. (For a calm input, expect a value near 0.)

---

## Integration

However you built your judge — Path A, B, or C — the **Integration** tab gives you a ready-to-use snippet.

- Switch between **cURL / Python / TypeScript**.
- Your `<experiment_id>/<version>` and **API key are prefilled**.
- Copy it with one click and drop it into your app — the endpoint serves traffic immediately.

**cURL example**

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.withemissary.com/v1/classification" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: <YOUR_API_KEY>" \
  -d '{
    "model": "<experiment_id>/<version>",
    "input": "I am so mad!",
    "data_format": "probs"
  }'
```

**Response**

```json
{
    "id": "classify-74a272b4396146bca318969acc1c4080",
    "model": "<experiment_id>/<version>",
    "data": [{ "index": 0, "probs": { "anger": 0.96 } }],
    "created": 1780077435
}
```

That's it — your judge is live wherever you need it.

# Experiments: zero-shot LLM deployments in minutes

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/experiment

**Experiment** is the fastest way to try the Emissary platform. In under a minute, you can spin up a customized model and call it from your application through a ready-made API endpoint — no training data, no tuning, no infrastructure setup required.

Every experiment starts as a **zero-shot model** built from the class definitions you provide. You can begin sending traffic immediately, then iterate by uploading data, labeling, and re-training as your use case matures.

Experiment currently supports six modes:

| Mode | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`judge`](#judge--llm-as-judge) | Evaluate outputs against a single criterion (LLM-as-Judge) |
| [`decision`](#decision) | Classify inputs into one of several mutually exclusive categories |
| [`routing`](#routing) | Route requests to the right downstream model, agent, or workflow |
| [`tool_calling`](#tool_calling) | Pick the right tool and extract its arguments from a user query |
| [`regression`](#regression) | Score inputs on a continuous numeric scale |
| [`ner`](#ner--text-extraction) | Extract named entities (people, places, custom types) from text |

---

## Common Workflow

Each mode follows the same two-step pattern:

1. **Create the experiment** by `POST`ing to `/v1/experiments` with a `mode` and a list of `classes`. You receive an `id` and `latest_version`.
2. **Call the model** at the mode's inference endpoint using the format `EXPERIMENT_ID/VERSION` as the `model` parameter.

All requests require your API key in the `X-API-Key` header.

---

## judge — LLM-as-Judge

Score a model's output against a single quality criterion. The model returns a probability that the criterion holds, which you can threshold or log for offline analysis.

**Use it for:** automated evaluation of LLM outputs in CI, online quality monitoring of a production assistant (helpfulness, safety, groundedness), or filtering low-quality generations from a synthetic dataset.

**Create the experiment:**

```python

response = requests.post(
    'https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': YOUR_API_KEY
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'MyJudge',
        'mode': 'judge',
        'classes': [
            {'name': 'helpful', 'description': 'Is the response to the query helpful?'}
        ]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

## decision

Classify an input into exactly one of several mutually exclusive labels. The model returns a probability distribution across all classes that sums to 1.

**Use it for:** sentiment analysis, intent detection, content moderation, support ticket triage, or any task where each input belongs to one and only one category.

**Create the experiment:**

```python
response = requests.post(
    'https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': YOUR_API_KEY
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'MyDecision',
        'mode': 'decision',
        'classes': [
            {'name': 'positive', 'description': 'The text expresses a positive sentiment, satisfaction, or approval.'},
            {'name': 'negative', 'description': 'The text expresses a negative sentiment, dissatisfaction, or complaint.'},
            {'name': 'neutral',  'description': 'The text is factual or does not express a strong opinion.'}
        ]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

```bash
curl https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $YOUR_API_KEY" \

    "mode": "decision",
    "classes": [
      {"name": "positive", "description": "The text expresses a positive sentiment, satisfaction, or approval."},
```

## routing

A specialized form of classification designed for picking the right downstream destination for each request. Behaves like `decision` but is optimized for routing patterns where each class represents a target model, agent, or pipeline.

**Use it for:** sending simple queries to a fast/cheap model and complex ones to a larger one, dispatching tasks across specialized agents (research, coding, creative), or routing customer messages to the correct team.

**Create the experiment:**

```python
response = requests.post(
    'https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': YOUR_API_KEY
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'MyRouter',
        'mode': 'routing',
        'classes': [
            {'name': 'simple_task',   'description': 'Simple, straightforward queries that can be handled by a small, fast model.'},
            {'name': 'complex_task',  'description': 'Complex queries requiring reasoning, code generation, or multi-step analysis.'},
            {'name': 'creative_task', 'description': 'Creative writing, brainstorming, or content generation tasks.'}
        ]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

```bash
curl https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "MyRouter",
    "mode": "routing",
    "classes": [
      {"name": "simple_task",   "description": "Simple, straightforward queries that can be handled by a small, fast model."},
      {"name": "complex_task",  "description": "Complex queries requiring reasoning, code generation, or multi-step analysis."},
      {"name": "creative_task", "description": "Creative writing, brainstorming, or content generation tasks."}

  }'
```

## tool_calling

Select the right tool for a user query *and* extract the arguments needed to call it. Each class is a tool defined with a JSON Schema for its parameters; the model returns both the tool's probability and a structured `generation` payload ready to pass to your function.

**Use it for:** building lightweight, low-latency function-calling agents without a general-purpose LLM in the hot path — database query dispatchers, API gateways, voice assistants, or any system where you need both routing and structured argument extraction in one call.

**Create the experiment:**

```python
response = requests.post(
    'https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': YOUR_API_KEY
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'MyToolCalling',
        'mode': 'tool_calling',
        'classes': [
            {
                'name': 'sql.execute',
                'description': 'Execute SQL queries based on user-defined parameters like SQL keyword, table name, column names, and conditions.',
                'parameters': {
                    'type': 'object',
                    'properties': {
                        'sql_keyword': {'type': 'string', 'enum': ['SELECT', 'INSERT', 'UPDATE', 'DELETE', 'CREATE']},
                        'table_name':  {'type': 'string'},
                        'columns':     {'type': 'array', 'items': {'type': 'string'}}
                    },
                    'required': ['sql_keyword', 'table_name']
                }
            },
            {
                'name': 'Movies_3_FindMovies',
                'description': 'Retrieves a list of movies based on the director, genre, and cast specified by the user.',
                'parameters': {
                    'type': 'object',
                    'properties': {
                        'directed_by': {'type': 'string'},
                        'genre':       {'type': 'string', 'enum': ['Fantasy', 'Mystery', 'Thriller', 'Comedy', 'Drama', 'Action']},
                        'cast':        {'type': 'string'}
                    },
                    'required': []
                }
            },
            {
                'name': 'Weather_1_GetWeather',
                'description': 'Retrieves the weather forecast for a specified city on a particular date.',
                'parameters': {
                    'type': 'object',
                    'properties': {
                        'city': {'type': 'string'},
                        'date': {'type': 'string'}
                    },
                    'required': ['city']
                }
            }
        ]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

```bash

  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "MyToolCalling",
    "mode": "tool_calling",
    "classes": [
      {
        "name": "sql.execute",
        "description": "Execute SQL queries based on user-defined parameters like SQL keyword, table name, column names, and conditions.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "sql_keyword": {"type": "string", "enum": ["SELECT", "INSERT", "UPDATE", "DELETE", "CREATE"]},
            "table_name":  {"type": "string"},
            "columns":     {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}
          },
          "required": ["sql_keyword", "table_name"]
        }
      },
      {
        "name": "Movies_3_FindMovies",
        "description": "Retrieves a list of movies based on the director, genre, and cast specified by the user.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "directed_by": {"type": "string"},
            "genre":       {"type": "string", "enum": ["Fantasy", "Mystery", "Thriller", "Comedy", "Drama", "Action"]},
            "cast":        {"type": "string"}
          },
          "required": []
```

```json
        "generation": [{
            "directed_by": "Christopher Nolan",
            "genre": "Action"
        }],

            "sql.execute":           0.0039021370466798544
        }
    }],

}
```

> **Note:** A built-in `NO_TOOL` class is added automatically so the model can decline to call any tool when none applies.

## regression

Score inputs on a continuous scale rather than choosing a discrete label. You define each scale by its min/max range and what the endpoints mean; the model returns a single numeric value.

**Use it for:** scoring sentiment intensity, response quality on a 1–5 scale, urgency or risk levels, readability, toxicity severity — anything where "how much" matters more than "which category."

**Create the experiment:**

```python
response = requests.post(
    'https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': YOUR_API_KEY
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'MyRegressor',
        'mode': 'regression',
        'classes': [{
            'name': 'valence',
            'description': 'How positive the emotional tone is.',
            'min_value': 0,
            'max_value': 1,
            'low_description':  'very negative emotional tone',
            'high_description': 'very positive emotional tone',
            'higher_means':     'more positive emotional tone'
        }]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

```bash
curl https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "MyRegressor",
    "mode": "regression",
    "classes": [{
      "name": "valence",
      "description": "How positive the emotional tone is.",
      "min_value": 0,
      "max_value": 1,
      "low_description":  "very negative emotional tone",
      "high_description": "very positive emotional tone",
      "higher_means":     "more positive emotional tone"

  }'
```

## ner — Text Extraction

Extract structured entities from unstructured text. Unlike a classifier, NER returns spans of text grouped by type, and you fully define what counts as an entity through the class descriptions — so you're not limited to a fixed taxonomy like PERSON/ORG/LOC.

**Use it for:** pulling structured data from emails, contracts, or chat messages; extracting PII for redaction; lifting custom entities like ticker symbols, drug names, product SKUs, or contract clauses from your domain.

**Create the experiment:**

```python
response = requests.post(
    'https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments',
    headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': YOUR_API_KEY
    },
    data=json.dumps({
        'name': 'MyExtractor',
        'mode': 'ner',
        'classes': [
            {'name': 'PERSON',       'description': 'human names'},
            {'name': 'ORGANIZATION', 'description': 'companies and institutions'},
            {'name': 'LOCATION',     'description': 'cities and places'}
        ]
    })
)
print(response.json())
```

```bash
curl https://api.withemissary.com/v1/experiments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "MyExtractor",
    "mode": "ner",
    "classes": [
      {"name": "PERSON",       "description": "human names"},
      {"name": "ORGANIZATION", "description": "companies and institutions"},
      {"name": "LOCATION",     "description": "cities and places"}
    ]
  }'
```

## Endpoint Reference

| Mode | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| `judge`, `decision`, `routing` | `POST /v1/classification` |
| `tool_calling` | `POST /v1/classify-generate` |
| `regression` | `POST /v1/regression` |
| `ner` | `POST /v1/ner` |

## Next Steps

The zero-shot model created here is just the starting point. Once you've validated the mode and class definitions against real traffic, you can:

- Upload labeled examples to fine-tune the model for higher accuracy
- Publish new versions and roll them out incrementally
- Monitor inference logs in the dashboard to spot edge cases

Head to the **Datasets** and **Training** sections of the docs to continue.

# What is model routing? LLM routers explained

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing

**Model routing** is the practice of choosing, for each request, which large language model (LLM)
should handle it. A **model router**, also called an **LLM router**, sits in front of a pool of
models, reads each request, and sends it to the model best suited to the job. Easy requests stop
paying for a frontier model, and hard requests stop getting stuck on a model that is weak at them.

```
            ┌──────────────────────────┐
request ───▶│       model router       │
            └─────────────┬────────────┘
                          │ one model per request
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        ▼                 ▼                 ▼
  small / fast       mid-size model    frontier model
     model
```

## How does model routing work?

Every routed request goes through the same three steps:

1. **Assess.** The router reads the request and estimates which models in the pool can do the task.
2. **Filter.** It keeps the models that are likely to succeed, and drops the ones that are not.
3. **Choose.** It picks one of the remaining models, usually the cheapest, and sends the request
   there.

On Emissary, the router gives each model a **confidence**: the probability that the model completes
this request. Models at or above your **confidence threshold** (0.80 by default) are the confident
pool, and the cheapest model in that pool serves the request. If no model is confident, the request
goes to your **default model**. Capability comes first and cost second, so savings never come from
accepting worse answers. See [how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision) for a
worked example.

## Why use model routing?

Most teams pick one model and send everything to it. Because that one model has to handle any
request, they pick a strong, expensive one. Easy requests overpay, and hard requests are limited by
whatever that single model happens to be bad at. Routing replaces the single choice with a decision
per request:

- **Better results than any single model.** Every model is better at some tasks and worse at
  others, and those strengths don't line up on one easy-to-hard scale.
- **Lower cost.** A cost reduction of **30–50%** is typical, and about **60%** of requests are
  usually served by a model other than the default. These are typical figures, not guarantees. See
  [how to reduce LLM costs with model routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/reduce-llm-costs).
- **Lower latency.** Smaller models respond sooner, and for agents that speed-up applies to every
  step that doesn't need a large model.
- **Easier model migration.** Adding or retiring a model doesn't mean rewriting application code.
  See [migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).
- **Insight into your workload.** Every decision records each model's confidence and the routing
  reason. See [what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).

The full argument is in [why route](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route).

## What are the types of model routers?

Routers differ along a few dimensions. The ones that matter most:

| Dimension | One end | Other end |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it optimizes for** | **Complexity-based:** guesses how hard the task is, then picks a cheap or an expensive model | **Performance-based:** asks which models can actually do the task |
| **What it knows about the models** | **Blind:** a small decision model trained on labeled queries | **Model-aware:** trained on rollouts of each model, with one head per model |
| **State** | **Stateless:** each decision is made in isolation | **Stateful:** uses cache state, so long conversations and agent loops don't throw away paid-for context |
| **Modality** | **Modality-blind:** treats every request as text | **Modality-aware:** knows which models accept images |
| **Cost** | **Per-token price only** | **Intelligence-density aware:** prices in how many output tokens each model will need |

Emissary's router is performance-based, model-aware, stateful, modality-aware and
intelligence-density aware. See [the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space) for
what each of these means, and [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees) for
the signals it uses.

## What is the difference between a model router and an LLM gateway?

A **gateway** is infrastructure for *how* requests reach models: one interface over many providers,
credentials, retries, rate limits, load balancing and failover. A **router** decides *which model*
should handle each request. Many products do only one of the two. Emissary is a router that also
works as a gateway: one URL, compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, with a router behind it.
You can also use its routing decision alongside a gateway you already run. See
[routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways).

## When should you not use model routing?

Routing is **online model selection**, made at request time. If you can select the model
**offline**, do. When the steps of your system are fixed and each step's input is narrow and
predictable, evaluate candidate models for each step and pin one. Routing is for the open-ended
parts: chat, agents, and anything where you can't list every kind of request ahead of time. See
[when to route, and when not to](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#when-to-route-and-when-not-to).

## How do you get started with model routing?

1. [Create a router](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started) in the Emissary dashboard: choose your models, add your own
   provider keys, and set a default model and a confidence threshold.
2. [Connect your app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect) by changing two things: the base URL and the
   `model` string. The gateway works with the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, curl, and coding agents
   such as Claude Code.
3. [Read the routing decisions](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug) in Activity to see each model's
   confidence and why the request went where it did.
4. [Run a trial on your own traffic](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial) before moving production traffic.

## How does Emissary compare with other routers?

See [compare LLM routers](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison) for Emissary side by side with
OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Not Diamond and Router.com, and the
[router selection checklist](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/selection-checklist) for questions to ask of any router.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does model routing reduce quality?

It shouldn't, and it can improve it. A performance-based router only sends a request to a model that
it is confident can complete it, and ranks by cost only among those models. Models are strong at
different things, so routing each request to the model that handles it best can outperform any
single model on your workload as a whole.

### How much can model routing save?

A cost reduction of 30–50% is typical. The bottom of that range is typical when routing within one
provider's model family, and the top when routing across open-source and closed-source models. Your
result depends on your traffic, catalog and default model, so measure it on your own requests.

### Does a router add latency?

A routing decision takes a little time, around 100 ms, and requests that go to a faster model finish
sooner. For multi-step agents, one deflection to a smaller model in a ten-step process can make up
the difference. Measure end-to-end latency on your workload rather than the routing step alone.

### Can I route across providers?

Yes. A router's catalog can span providers, for example Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter, using a
key you store for each. See [choose your models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models).

More questions are answered in the [model routing FAQ](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/faq).


---

# Why use model routing? Benefits and trade-offs

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route

**Route across models when your traffic varies in difficulty and your inputs are open-ended.** A
model router sends each request to the model best suited to it, so easy requests stop paying for a
frontier model and hard requests stop getting stuck on a weak one. Typical results are a 30–50% cost
reduction with quality held or improved. If you can choose a model ahead of time for every step,
don't route. See [what is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing) for the definition.

Most teams pick one model and send everything to it. Because they have to pick just one, they
**peak provision**: they choose the model that can handle *any* request, and use it for *every*
request, even though they know there is no such thing as one best model. That choice is a
compromise in both directions: easy requests overpay for intelligence they don't need, and hard
requests are limited by whatever that one model happens to be bad at.

**Model routing** replaces that single choice with a decision made per request. A **model router**
sits in front of a pool of models, looks at each request, and sends it to the model best suited to
handle it.

```
            ┌──────────────────────────┐
request ───▶│       model router       │
            └─────────────┬────────────┘
                          │ one model per request
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        ▼                 ▼                 ▼
  small / fast       mid-size model    frontier model
     model
```

## What are the benefits of model routing?
- **Best-of-all-worlds performance.** *There is no one best model.* Every model is better at some
  kinds of tasks and worse at others, and those strengths don't line up on a neat scale from easy to
  hard. A router that understands them sends each request to the model that does that kind of work
  best, so the combined result can beat *any single frontier model* on its own. It only sends a
  request to a model that is likely to complete it, so the savings below never come from accepting
  worse answers.

- **Lower cost.** Requests that a cheaper model can handle go to a cheaper model, so you stop paying
  for intelligence an easy request doesn't need. For long conversations and agent loops, the router
  saves more by taking the prompt cache and reasoning effort into account, so it doesn't throw away
  context it has already paid for. See
  [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees).

- **Lower latency.** Smaller models respond sooner, so routing an easy request to one finishes it
  faster. For agents, that speed-up applies to every step that doesn't need a large model. Routing
  adds some overhead of its own (~100ms), but a single deflection in a 10-step process can make up
  the difference, and average deflection rates approach 60%.

- **Seamless migration.** New models ship constantly. With a router, adding one to the pool, or
  retiring an old one, doesn't mean rewriting application code or re-testing every prompt by hand.
  The router also scores models you haven't enabled, so you can see when a new model could take a
  meaningful share of your traffic. See [migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).

- **Insight into your workload.** Every routing decision records how confident each model was and
  why the request went where it did. That gives you a view of your workload that a single-model setup
  can't: which requests are easy, which ones nothing can handle, and which models you're missing. See
  [what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).

- **A path to your own models.** Every routed request leaves a trajectory. Over time, you can serve
  the open models you rely on from dedicated capacity tuned to your traffic, and post-train models of
  your own on that traffic. The router sends work to them when they're the better call, so routing
  feeds your training data and training makes routing cheaper. See
  [from routing to your own models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights#from-routing-to-your-own-models).

## How much does model routing save?
- **30–50% cost reduction** is typical. The more options you give the router, the more it saves,
  and where you land in that range depends on what's in your catalog:
  - **Bottom of the range** when routing *within a family of models*, for example across the sizes
    of one provider's lineup.
  - **Top of the range** when routing *across open-source and closed-source models*, since open
    models widen the gap between the cheapest capable model and the default.
- **~60% deflection from the default model**, meaning about 60% of requests are served by a model
  other than the default. This is usually measured against a default of Opus 5.x-grade models.

These are typical figures, not guarantees. They depend on your traffic, catalog and default model,
so measure on your own requests. See [run a trial](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial). Once a router has
traffic, the **Saved** figure in Activity shows spend against a baseline of the default model. See
[monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug#activity).

## What does the value of routing depend on?
The value depends on the quality of the routing decision. A router that is wrong too often either
sends hard requests to weak models, and quality drops, or plays it safe and sends everything to the
largest model, and there are no savings. How Emissary's router avoids both is covered in
[how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

Routing isn't right for every workload. The last section of this page covers when not to use it.

## When should you route, and when not?
Routing is **online model selection**: the model is chosen at request time, per step. The
alternative is **offline model selection**: you choose the model ahead of time and pin it. The rule
of thumb is that **if you can select the model offline, do.** Routing exists for the cases where you
can't know in advance what a request will need. Its worth keeping in mind that the same aspect of AI that makes it so accessible - a unified front door, makes it harder to pin models.

### Why offline selection is valuable when it's possible

A router makes its decision at request time, under uncertainty, and it has to handle whatever
arrives. If you already know what each step of your system does, you can do that work ahead of
time: evaluate candidate models on that step, pick one, and pin it. There's no runtime decision to get wrong, and no routing step to pay for.

You can select offline when your steps are **predefined**. That's more akin to a **workflow** rather than an
**agent**: the sequence of steps is fixed, and each step has little flexibility in what it receives.
For a step like that, you don't need a broad open front door. You need the one model that does that
one job well over and over again. 

### Workflow or agent?

| Your system | What the input looks like | Model selection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Workflow** with fixed steps, such as extract fields, classify, summarize | Narrow and predictable at each step | **Offline**: pick a model per step and pin it |
| **Agent or open-ended product** | Anything a user or a loop might send | **Online**: route |
| **Mixed**: a workflow with a few open-ended steps | Predictable in most places, open in a few | Pin the predictable steps, route the open ones |

### Where routing wins

Online selection is the right tool when:

- **Inputs are open-ended.** Users, agents, and tool outputs can send anything, and you can't
  classify the traffic ahead of time.
- **Difficulty varies a lot** within the same entry point, so some requests need a frontier model
  and many don't.
- **Models change often**, and you don't want to re-run model selection every time one ships.
- **You want to learn what your traffic looks like.** Routing decisions show you which requests
  are easy, which are hard, and which none of your models handle with confidence. See
  [what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).

### Quick check

Before you set up a router, ask:

1. Can I list every kind of request this system will receive? If yes, select offline.
2. Is each step's input narrow and predictable? If yes, pin a model for that step.
3. Does anything open-ended sit in front of the system, such as chat, an agent, or search over
   arbitrary data? If yes, route that part.

## Where to go next

- [Get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started): create a router and send your first request.
- [How a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision): what happens to each request.


---

# How to reduce LLM costs with model routing

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/reduce-llm-costs

The most reliable way to reduce LLM API costs without lowering quality is to **stop sending every
request to the same expensive model**. Route each request to the **cheapest model that is confident
it can complete it**, and let cache state, output length and reasoning effort inform which model is
actually cheapest. A cost reduction of **30–50%** is typical. This page explains where the savings
come from and how to measure them on your own traffic.

## Why do LLM costs get so high?

Teams usually **peak provision**: they choose the one model that can handle *any* request and use it
for *every* request. Requests that a smaller model could handle pay for intelligence they don't
need. The bill is also shaped by things a per-token price list doesn't show:

- **Output length.** A model with a lower per-token price that needs far more tokens to answer can
  cost more overall.
- **Prompt caching.** Sending a long conversation to a model that already holds it in cache can
  cost far less than sending it to a nominally cheaper model that has to process it from scratch.
- **Reasoning effort.** Running a model at higher effort buys more reasoning at more cost and
  latency, whether or not the request needed it.
- **Your actual rates.** Contract discounts and provider markups change which model is cheapest.

## What are the levers for lowering LLM spend?

| Lever | What it does | Where it's covered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Right-size the model per request** | Easy requests go to cheaper models, and only requests that need a frontier model pay for one | [How a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision) |
| **Rank by expected cost, not list price** | Estimates output tokens per model, so a cheap model that rambles doesn't win | [What the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#expected-output-length) |
| **Respect the prompt cache** | Credits a model that already holds the context, so long conversations and agent loops don't throw away paid-for tokens | [What the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#cache-state) |
| **Choose the lowest sufficient effort** | A confident model is served at the lowest effort that clears the threshold, and changing effort keeps the cache | [What the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#effort) |
| **Use your real prices** | Ranking follows your contract rates, not list prices | [Use your own pricing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing) |

## How does Emissary's router lower cost without lowering quality?

It splits the decision in two. First it **protects quality**: the router estimates each model's
confidence that it can complete the request, and keeps only the models at or above your
[confidence threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold). Then it **optimizes cost**, only within that
set, by picking the cheapest confident model. If no model is confident, the request goes to your
default model, so the default is your safety net. A router that blends quality and cost into one
score can trade a quality loss for a saving without you noticing. See
[why capability comes before cost](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision#why-capability-comes-before-cost).

## How much will I save?

- **30–50% cost reduction** is typical. The more options you give the router, the more it saves.
  - **Bottom of the range** when routing within a family of models, for example across the sizes of
    one provider's lineup.
  - **Top of the range** when routing across open-source and closed-source models, since open
    models widen the gap between the cheapest capable model and the default.
- **About 60% deflection from the default model**: roughly 60% of requests are served by a model
  other than the default. This is usually measured against a default of Opus 5.x-grade models.

These are typical figures, not guarantees. A workload where most requests need a frontier model
saves less than one with many routine requests, and cache and effort decisions add savings for
agentic workloads.

## How do I measure the savings on my own traffic?

1. **Build a representative sample** of real requests, including easy, hard and odd ones. For
   agents, use whole multi-step runs.
2. **Set a baseline** by running the sample through your current setup and recording cost, latency
   and quality.
3. **Run the same sample through a router** and compare. Look at quality first, because savings that
   come with a quality drop aren't savings.
4. **Read the routing decisions** and adjust the threshold, catalog and pricing one change at a
   time.

See [run a trial on your traffic](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial) for the full procedure. Once a router has
traffic, the **Saved** figure in Activity shows spend against a baseline of your default model. See
[monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug#activity).

## When won't routing reduce my costs?

If almost every request needs the same model, routing won't help much. And if your workload is a
fixed workflow with predictable steps, you can pick and pin a model for each step ahead of time,
with no routing step to pay for. See
[when to route, and when not to](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#when-to-route-and-when-not-to).

## Next steps

- [What is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing) for the basics.
- [Get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started) to create your first router in about ten minutes.
- [Set the confidence threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold), the main quality-versus-cost dial.
