# Get started: create your first LLM router

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started

This takes about ten minutes. You'll create a router, send it a request, and check how that
request was routed. Anything that needs a decision links to a guide, so you can follow the short
path now and come back to tune later.

Routers are created and configured in the Emissary dashboard. For now, the initial setup can't be
done through the API. Once a router exists, you call it through the gateway API.

## Before you begin

- An Emissary account. Sign in at [withemissary.com](https://www.withemissary.com).
- An API key for each provider whose models you want in the router, for example Anthropic,
  OpenAI, or OpenRouter. Keys are stored encrypted and never returned to the browser.
- An **Emissary platform API key**, found under **Settings → Credentials**. You'll use it to call
  the gateway.

## 1. Create a router

In the dashboard, open **Router** and click **New router**.

1. **Name it.** Clients select a router by sending its name as the request's `model`, so it must
   be unique across your routers, for example `production-agents`.
2. **Choose data retention.** *Zero data retention* is on by default: Emissary does not retain
   input, output, or session replay data from gateway traffic, only routing decisions, token
   counts, and cost telemetry. **To get the most out of routing, turn zero data retention off.**
   Stored traffic is what lets you replay sessions, and it's the raw material for
   [what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights): a view of your workload, dedicated inference, and
   post-training on your own trajectories.
3. **Pick the models to route across.** Toggle on each model you want and choose its provider.
   Not sure which? Start from a [power package](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models).
4. **Add provider credentials.** A key field appears for each provider your selected models use.
   For open-source models, Emissary currently invokes them through OpenRouter. Select OpenRouter,
   and if you'd rather use a different gateway, change the base URL to point to it.
5. **Set the routing policy.** Choose a **default model** and leave the **confidence threshold**
   at its default of 0.80 for now. See [choose your models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models) and
   [set the confidence threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold).
6. Click **Create configuration**.

## 2. Send a request

Send your router's name as the `model`, with your Emissary platform API key. Edit the fields
below, then click **Run** to send a request from this page, or **Copy curl** to run it in a terminal.

The gateway is compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs. For the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, Go,
Node.js, and coding agents such as Claude Code, see
[connect an app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect).

## 3. See how it was routed

Open your router in the dashboard and go to **Activity**. Click into a request to see each model's
confidence and the reason the router chose the model it did. See
[monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).

The router's **Configuration** tab shows what you set up, including each target model's pricing and
which provider keys are stored. You can also edit it there: change the default model, add or remove
models, and change the confidence threshold.

## Next steps

- [How a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision) explains what you just saw in
  Activity.
- [Run a trial on your traffic](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial) before moving production traffic.
- [When to route, and when not to](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#when-to-route-and-when-not-to) if you're not sure routing fits a
  given part of your system.


---

# How an LLM router decides which model to use

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision

Every request to an Emissary router goes through the same decision. In short: **find the models
that can do the job, then pick the cheapest of them.** Capability first, cost second.

## How does the router decide, step by step?
### 1. Estimate each model's confidence

The router's classifier reads the request and gives each model a **confidence**: how likely that
model is to complete the task. It has **one head per model and effort level**, so it estimates the
probability that a model passes this request *at that effort*. It can do this because it was
**post-trained on thousands of rollouts** of these models, so it has seen what each one does well
and badly. See [the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space) for why that matters.

The classifier scores every model it knows, not only the ones in your catalog. Your catalog decides
which models are *candidates* for serving the request. The rest still get a score, which is how you
find out about models you haven't enabled. See
[migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).

### 2. Keep the confident models

You set a **confidence threshold**, 0.80 by default. A model is **confident** when any of its
effort levels clears the threshold. The confident models in your catalog are the **confident pool**
for this request. Raising the threshold makes the router more conservative, and lowering it saves
more but accepts more risk. See [set the confidence threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold).

### 3. Pick the cheapest confident model

Among the confident models, the router ranks by expected cost. For each one it works out:

- the **price**, including any pricing you've customized,
- the **expected output length** for that model on this task,
- the **cache state**, so a model that already holds the context is credited for it,
- and the **effort** level: a confident model is served at the **lowest effort that clears the
  threshold**, since less effort means less reasoning cost, and the same model keeps its cache.

The cheapest wins. See [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees) for each of these.

### 4. Fall back or escalate when needed

Your **default model** is the anchor. Two cases move the decision away from a plain "cheapest
confident":

- **No model is confident.** The request goes to the default model, and the routing reason is
  recorded as `default_no_confident`.
- **The default isn't confident but a pricier model is.** The request is **escalated** to the more
  expensive model that can vouch for the task.

```
request ─▶ confidence per model ─▶ ≥ threshold? ─┬─ some models ─▶ cheapest of them
                                                 │                (cheapest_confident)
                                                 └─ none ─▶ default model
                                                            (default_no_confident)
```

Every decision records the classifier's probability for each model and effort, an estimated cost
per candidate, and the routing reason, so you can see why any request went where it did. See [monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).

## Why does capability come before cost?
Splitting the decision this way keeps quality and cost separate. The first stage protects quality
by filtering to models that can do the job. The second optimizes cost, only within that set. A
router that mixes them into a single score can trade a quality loss for a cost saving without you
noticing.

It's also the difference between **performance-based** and **complexity-based** routing. A
complexity-based router guesses how hard a task is from the input, then picks a cheap or an
expensive model, and complexity is hard to read from the input alone. Emissary asks which models
can actually do the task, based on how they've performed. See
[the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space#what-the-router-optimizes-for).

## Worked example

*The numbers here are illustrative. They show the mechanics, not real measurements.*

A router has three models, a default of `claude-opus-5.5`, and a threshold of 0.80.

| Model | Price per Mtok (in / out) |
| --- | --- |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash` | $0.15 / $0.6 |
| `claude-sonnet-5.5` | $2 / $10 |
| `claude-opus-5.5` (default) | $4 / $20 |

Three requests arrive:

| | `deepseek-v4.1-flash` | `claude-sonnet-5.5` | `claude-opus-5.5` | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A.** Routine edit in a long agent run | 0.52 | 0.91 | 0.97 | `claude-sonnet-5.5`: confident and cheaper than the default |
| **B.** Very hard, unusual task | 0.41 | 0.63 | 0.78 | `claude-opus-5.5`: none confident, so the default serves (`default_no_confident`) |
| **C.** Simple lookup | 0.93 | 0.96 | 0.98 | `deepseek-v4.1-flash`: confident and cheapest |

For request A, two models clear the threshold, `claude-sonnet-5.5` and `claude-opus-5.5`. Both
are confident, so cost decides. `claude-sonnet-5.5` is cheaper per token, and if the conversation
is already cached on it, cheaper still. It wins.

Request B is the interesting one for your own tuning. If a lot of traffic looks like B, no model
in the catalog can vouch for it. That's a signal to add a stronger model, or to post-train one for
that kind of task. See [from routing to your own models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights#from-routing-to-your-own-models).

## What this means for you

- **Quality is a setting, not a side effect.** The threshold, not the cost ranking, controls how
  much risk the router accepts.
- **The default model is your safety net.** Pick one you'd trust with any request, because it
  serves everything nothing else is confident about. See
  [choose your models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models).
- **Every decision can be audited.** Confidence and reason are recorded per request.


---

# What an LLM router sees: cache, effort and cost

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees

A router that only reads the request text can only guess. Emissary's router also sees the situation
around the request, and that's what lets it find the cheapest *good* option rather than the
cheapest *nominal* one. This page covers each signal. For how they combine into a decision, see
[how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

## Cache state

*Also called: stateful routing.*

Prompt caching changes the economics of a request. Sending a long conversation to a model that
already holds it in cache can be far cheaper than sending it to a nominally cheaper model that has
to process it from scratch. A router that can't see cache state can't make that tradeoff.

Emissary's router knows what each model has cached and takes it into account. Each target model's
cache read and write prices are part of its configuration, so cached context is priced in.

## Expected output length

*Also called: intelligence density.*

Models differ in how many output tokens they need to complete the same task. A model with a lower
per-token price that needs far more tokens to answer can cost more overall. The router estimates
how many output tokens each model will need for the task and prices that in, instead of comparing
per-token prices alone.

## Effort

Emissary routes across **models and effort**, not just models. Many models can run at different
effort levels, trading more reasoning for more cost and latency. For a request that doesn't need a
different model, the router can change the effort instead.

The classifier has **one head per model and effort**, for example `@low`, `@medium`, and `@high`
for a model that supports them. Each head is the probability that the model passes the request at
that effort. A model is confident when any effort clears the confidence threshold, and it's served
at the **lowest effort that does**. Models without effort levels have a single head and run at the
provider's default effort.

This matters because it **preserves the cache.** Prompt cache lives with the model, so switching
models forfeits whatever the previous model had cached. Staying on the same model and changing the
effort keeps it warm. A router that can see cache state prefers the cheaper move: adjust effort
first, and switch models only when the capability gain is worth losing the cache.

Where effort routing applies to a model, the **Effort routing** column in the router's
Configuration tab shows it.

## Modality

A router needs to know which models can accept which inputs. The router knows which models handle
images, shown in the **Vision** column of the Configuration tab, so it never sends an image request
to a text-only model. Being modality-aware doesn't mean the router interprets the image content.
That is a further step, called *multimodal* routing. See [the design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space).

## Your pricing

The ranking uses the prices on your router: input, output, and cache read and write, per model.
Pricing is prefilled with list prices, and you can change it to match your contracts. That way the
router's idea of "cheapest" is *your* cheapest. See [use your own pricing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing).

## Context limits

Each model's context window is part of its configuration, so a request that's too long for a model
isn't routed there.

## Which signals does the router use?
| Signal | What it prevents |
| --- | --- |
| Cache state | Paying to re-process context another model already holds |
| Expected output length | Choosing a "cheap" model that costs more once it answers |
| Effort | Losing the cache by switching models when changing effort would do |
| Modality | Sending an image to a model that can't read it |
| Your pricing | Optimizing for list prices you don't actually pay |


---

# Types of LLM routers: the router design space

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space

Routers aren't all the same kind of thing. This page maps the main ways they differ. It's neutral
background, useful for evaluating any router, and the
[comparisons](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-notdiamond) and the
[selection checklist](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/selection-checklist) build on it. For how Emissary's own router
works, see [how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

## What the router optimizes for

**Complexity-based routing** estimates how hard a task is, then routes to a cheap or an expensive
model accordingly. It rests on an assumption that is hard to meet: that you can tell how complex a
task is *from the input alone*. A short prompt can require deep reasoning and a long one can be
routine, so complexity estimates are often wrong in both directions.

**Performance-based routing** doesn't ask how hard the task is. It asks which models can do it.
Model capabilities form a **jagged frontier**: a smaller model may beat a larger one on some tasks
and fail on others, and that doesn't line up with a single easy-to-hard scale. A performance-based
router learns the strengths and weaknesses of each model and routes along that frontier.

| | Complexity-based | Performance-based |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Question it answers** | How hard is this task? | Which models can do this task? |
| **Assumes** | Models sit on one cheap-to-expensive scale | Each model has its own strengths and weaknesses |
| **Main weakness** | Complexity is hard to estimate from the input | Needs evidence of how each model performs |
| **Trained on** | Query labels or complexity scores | Rollouts of each model in the pool |

## How much the router knows about the models

### Blind: a small decision model

The simplest router is a small **decision model** that reads the query and predicts which of *N*
models it should go to, trained on labeled examples. It's cheap and fast, but it is **blind to what
it's routing**. It learns a mapping from query text to a label, with no direct evidence of how each
model performs. When models are added or change, the labels go stale.

### Model-aware: one head per model

A more technical approach plays out a large number of **trajectories** with each candidate model
and trains the decision model on that distribution. The decision model has **one head per model**,
and each head learns the likelihood that *its* model can complete the task. The router is now
**aware of what it is routing**. It isn't asking "what does this query look like?" but "given what
I've seen this model do, will it succeed here?"

## What state the router tracks

A **stateless** router makes each decision in isolation, and doesn't know what it's done before. A
**stateful** router knows the current situation, most importantly **cache state**, and uses it.
Prompt caching changes which option is cheapest, so a stateless router can pick the wrong model
for a long conversation. See [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#cache-state).

## What the router knows about inputs

- **Modality-blind** routers treat every request as text.
- **Modality-aware** routers know which models can handle images, even if they can't interpret the
  images.
- **Multimodal** routers also use the image content in the decision.

Modality-aware does not imply multimodal.

## What the router knows about cost

A router that compares only per-token prices is **intelligence-density unaware**. An
**intelligence-density aware** router estimates how many output tokens a model will need for a task
and prices that in. See [what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#expected-output-length).

## Summary

| Dimension | One end | Other end |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Optimizes for** | Complexity | Performance |
| **Model awareness** | Blind | Aware (trained on rollouts) |
| **State** | Stateless | Stateful (cache-aware) |
| **Modality** | Modality-blind | Modality-aware, then multimodal |
| **Cost** | Per-token price only | Intelligence-density aware |

Emissary's router sits at the right-hand end of the first four rows and is intelligence-density
aware. It is performance-based, model-aware, stateful and modality-aware, not multimodal.


---

# LLM router vs LLM gateway: the difference

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways

A **gateway** is infrastructure for *how* requests reach models. It gives you one interface over
many providers and typically handles credentials, retries, timeouts, rate limits, load balancing,
logging, and failover. It sends each request to the model *you*, or your rules, specified.

A **router** decides *which model* should handle each request. It makes a per-request decision
based on what the request needs, and optimizes for cost, latency, or quality.

| | Gateway | Router |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Question it answers** | How do I reach and manage models? | Which model should answer this request? |
| **Typical features** | Keys, retries, fallbacks, load balancing, observability | Capability prediction, cost ranking |
| **Decision basis** | Config and rules | The request itself, and for stateful routers, the current state |

Many products do one of these. A pure gateway has no opinion about which model is right, and a
pure router returns a recommendation and leaves execution to you.

## Emissary can be both

Emissary is a router, and it can also be your gateway. You choose how to use it:

| | **Router and gateway** (recommended) | **Routing policy alongside your gateway** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **How it works** | Your apps call Emissary, which decides which model serves the request and makes the call | You keep your existing gateway, and Emissary supplies the routing decision |
| **What you change** | The base URL and the `model` string | Your gateway's routing step |
| **Who calls the provider** | Emissary, on your provider keys | Your gateway |
| **Simplicity** | One URL, one place for keys and config | Two systems to keep in step |
| **Insights** | Full: Emissary sees each request from start to finish | Limited to what Emissary sees |

### Emissary as the router and the gateway

We recommend this. An Emissary router comes with a gateway:

- **One gateway URL** for all your agents and applications.
- **Wire-compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs**, so you use the official SDKs, any
  compatible library, or plain HTTP.
- **Your own provider keys.** Calls to model providers use keys you've stored, encrypted, in the
  router's configuration.
- **A router behind the URL.** Each router is a model catalog and a routing policy of its own, and
  you address it by sending its name as the request's `model`.

The same call that reaches your models also makes the routing decision, so there's no separate
service to call for a recommendation and then execute yourself.

```
your app ──▶ one gateway URL ──▶ router "production-agents" ──▶ chosen model ──▶ provider
              model: "production-agents"   (decide)                (call, on your keys)
```

**Why we recommend it.** It makes everything simpler, with one URL to point at and one place to
manage keys, models, and pricing. It also gives you better insights. When Emissary handles the
whole request, it sees the outcome as well as the decision: cost, cache hits, latency, tokens, and
whole sessions. That's what powers [Activity and Metrics](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug) and
[what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).

### Emissary alongside your gateway

If you already run a gateway and want to keep it, Emissary can sit alongside it as the **routing
policy**. Your gateway keeps doing what it does today, such as credentials, retries, and failover,
and Emissary decides which model should serve each request. This suits teams with a gateway they
rely on or can't change.

You get the routing decision, and the savings that follow from it. Insights are limited to what
Emissary can see from its side of the request.

## Where this matters in practice

- **Switching from a single model:** change the base URL and the `model` string. See
  [connect an app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect).
- **Comparing products:** some gateways have routing features, but those are usually rules and
  fallbacks rather than per-request capability prediction. See the
  [comparisons](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-litellm).
- **Routing across providers you already use:** a router's catalog can span providers, for example
  Anthropic, OpenAI, and OpenRouter, using a key for each.


---

# Choose models for your LLM router catalog

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models

Your router's **catalog** is the set of models it can route across. A wider catalog gives the
router more strengths to route along, which is where
[best-of-all-worlds performance](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#what-you-get) comes from.
A narrower one is simpler to reason about and needs fewer provider keys.

Pick models in the **Models** section of the New router form. Model names are fixed because they
double as the router's classifier labels, so the only required choice per model is the provider.
Pricing and limits are prefilled, and you can [adjust them](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing).

## Power packages

Three starting points. Toggle on the models in the form, using the names below. Prices are the
prefilled list prices per million input / output tokens.

### Open-source only

For teams that want open-weights models only.

| Model | Price per Mtok (in / out) |
| --- | --- |
| `kimi-k3` | $3 / $15 |
| `glm-5.3` | $1.4 / $4.4 |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash` | $0.15 / $0.6 |

### Closed-source only

For teams that want proprietary frontier models only.

| Model | Price per Mtok (in / out) |
| --- | --- |
| `claude-opus-5` | $5 / $25 |
| `claude-sonnet-5.5` | $2 / $10 |
| `gpt-5.6-luna` | $0.2 / $1.2 |

### Open and closed

The widest catalog, for the best mix of capability and cost.

| Model | Price per Mtok (in / out) |
| --- | --- |
| `claude-opus-5.5` | $4 / $20 |
| `claude-sonnet-5.5` | $2 / $10 |
| `gpt-6.1-sol` | $2 / $10 |
| `glm-5.3` | $1.4 / $4.4 |
| `gpt-6-luna` | $0.1 / $0.5 |
| `deepseek-v4.1-flash` | $0.15 / $0.6 |

You'll need a provider key for each provider the selected models use. For open-source models,
Emissary currently invokes them through OpenRouter. Select OpenRouter as the provider, and if you'd
rather use a different gateway, change the base URL to point to any other one.

Model availability and prices change, so check the form for the current list.

## Choose a default model

The **default model** is the anchor of the routing policy. It's required, and it serves any request
that no model is confident about, recorded as `default_no_confident`. Pricier confident models can
also take a request from it by escalation. See
[how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision#4-fall-back-or-escalate-when-needed).

That makes it your safety net, so pick a model you'd trust with *any* request in your workload, not
the cheapest one. In the packages above, that usually means one of the larger models.

## Tips

- **Start with a package, then adjust.** You can change the catalog later with **Edit
  configuration**.
- **Mix price points.** A catalog of only expensive models leaves little room to save, and one of
  only cheap models leaves the router nothing to escalate to.
- **Cover your modalities.** If you send images, make sure the catalog has models that support
  vision. The Configuration tab's **Vision** column shows which do.
- **Add models as they ship.** See [migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).


---

# Confidence threshold: quality vs cost in routing

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold

The **confidence threshold** is the setting that most affects the quality and cost of your router.
It's how confident the router must be that a model can complete a request before that model is
allowed to serve it. The default is **0.80**.

## What it does

For each request the router gives every model a confidence. Models at or above the threshold are in
the confident pool, and the cheapest of them serves the request. See
[how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

- **A higher threshold is more conservative.** Fewer models clear the bar, so fewer requests go to
  cheaper models and more fall back to the default model or escalate. Quality risk drops, and so do
  the savings.
- **A lower threshold saves more.** More models clear the bar, so more requests go to cheaper
  models, with more risk that a cheaper model isn't up to the task.

## How to tune it

1. **Start at the default (0.80)** and send representative traffic.
2. **Look at the routing reasons** in [Activity](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug). A large share of
   `default_no_confident` means the threshold is high for your catalog, or that your catalog
   doesn't cover this traffic. Lowering the threshold helps in the first case, and adding models in
   the second.
3. **Check quality, not just cost.** Compare outputs against your current setup on a sample of
   your own requests. See [run a trial on your traffic](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial).
4. **Change it in small steps** and re-check. In the router's **Configuration** tab, use **Edit
   configuration**.

## What the threshold doesn't do

It doesn't change how models are ranked once they're in the confident pool. That's decided by price,
expected output length, cache state and effort. See
[what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees). It only decides who gets into the
pool.


---

# Use your own LLM pricing in a router

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing

The router picks the cheapest confident model, so what it believes things cost matters. If your
rates differ from list prices, because of a committed-spend discount, a negotiated contract, or a
provider route with its own markup, tell the router, and its rankings will follow your real costs.

## What's on a model's price

Each target model on your router carries:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Input $/Mtok** | Price per million input tokens |
| **Output $/Mtok** | Price per million output tokens |
| **Cache R/W $/Mtok** | Price per million tokens to read from, and write to, the prompt cache |
| **Context** | The model's context window |
| **Vision** | Whether the model accepts images |
| **Effort routing** | Whether the router can adjust effort for the model |

Prices are prefilled when you add a model. They show next to each model in the New router form and
in the **Target models** table on the Configuration tab.

## Change them

1. Open the router and go to **Configuration**.
2. Click **Edit configuration**.
3. Adjust a model's pricing, and save.

Cache read and write prices matter more than they look. The router credits a model that already
holds your context in cache, so an accurate cache price is what makes
[cache-aware routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#cache-state) choose well.

## Why it matters

A model that's the cheapest at list price might not be the cheapest at the price you pay. If your
rates are different and the router doesn't know, it'll rank on the wrong numbers.


---

# Migrate to new LLMs with model routing

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models

New models ship constantly, and the usual way to adopt one is slow and uncertain: swap it in
somewhere, hand-test a few prompts, and hope. Routing gives you a better way.

## The router scores models you haven't enabled

Emissary's router predicts confidence across **all** models, including ones you haven't added to
your catalog. Over time that tells you something you'd otherwise have to find out by experiment:
when there's a model you aren't using that the router believes could handle a large share of your
requests.

So migration isn't a leap. You see the evidence first, then decide.

## A migration workflow

The safest way to adopt a new model is as an A/B experiment. Create a second router with the same
setup plus the new model, send it a share of your traffic, and compare it with your current router
before you commit.

1. **Notice the opportunity.** Open a request in Activity and look at **Classifier probabilities**.
   It lists every model the router scores, including ones outside your catalog. Look for a model
   you haven't enabled that is confident for a meaningful share of your traffic. See
   [what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).
2. **Create a second router.** Create a new router with the **same models, default model, and
   confidence threshold** as your current one, **plus the new model**. Add a key for the new
   model's provider if you don't have one yet. Keeping everything else identical means any
   difference you see comes from the new model. See [get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started).
3. **Check pricing.** Confirm the new model's [pricing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing) reflects your rates, since the
   router ranks on it.
4. **Send it some traffic.** Use the second router's name as the `model` for a portion of your
   requests, for example a small percentage, and keep the rest on your current router. Your
   application changes only in which router name it sends.
5. **Compare.** Put the two routers side by side in [Activity and Metrics](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug):
   spend, savings against baseline, latency, model mix, and routing reasons. Then check quality
   against your own measures. See [run a trial on your traffic](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial).
6. **Promote it.** If the new router does better, move all your traffic to it. Or add the new model
   to your original router with **Edit configuration**, so your application keeps using the same
   router name.

Once the new model is in your main router, your application needs no changes. Requests still go to
the same gateway URL with the same router name, and the router decides what serves them.

## Retiring a model

The same applies in reverse. If a model is deprecated or you want to drop a provider, remove it
from the catalog and the router stops sending it traffic. Nothing in your application refers to it.

## Why this works

Every request is already being classified for every model, so the router accumulates evidence on
how each one would have done on *your* traffic. A new model benchmark on someone else's tasks says
little about yours. Confidence on your own requests does.


---

# Connect an app or agent to an LLM router

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect

Every router is reached through one gateway URL. It's compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs,
so the official SDKs, any compatible library, and plain HTTP all work. You send your router's name
as the `model`, and authenticate with your **Emissary platform API key** from
**Settings → Credentials**.

To switch an existing integration, change two things: the base URL, and the `model` string.

The **Connect** tab on each router shows ready-to-copy examples with its name filled in.

## SDKs and HTTP

| API | Base URL |
| --- | --- |
| OpenAI-compatible (Chat Completions, Responses) | `https://api.withemissary.com/gateway/v1` |
| Anthropic-compatible (Messages) | `https://api.withemissary.com/gateway` |

### OpenAI SDK

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.withemissary.com/gateway/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_EMISSARY_API_KEY",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="my-router",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

### Anthropic SDK

```python

client = anthropic.Anthropic(
    base_url="https://api.withemissary.com/gateway",
    api_key="YOUR_EMISSARY_API_KEY",
)

message = client.messages.create(
    model="my-router",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(message.content[0].text)
```

### curl

```bash
curl https://api.withemissary.com/gateway/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_EMISSARY_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "model": "my-router",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
  }'
```

The Connect tab also shows examples for Node.js and Go, and for the Responses and Messages APIs.

## What comes back

The response is in the format of the API you called. Its `model` field reports the provider model
that served the request, such as `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`, so you can see which model the
router chose without opening the dashboard. Usage, including cost, comes back in the usual
`usage` field.

## Coding agents

Point a coding agent at the gateway and every request it makes is routed. For Claude Code, run
the following in your shell and then start it:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.withemissary.com/gateway
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='YOUR_EMISSARY_API_KEY'
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL='my-router'
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL='my-router'
claude
```

The Connect tab has setup instructions for Pi, Codex, Hermes, and omp as well.

## Sessions

Calls are grouped into **sessions** by an agent session header. Claude Code sends one
automatically, and other agents show up in Sessions once they send one. Calls without a session id
still appear in Activity, but can't be replayed. See [monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).


---

# Monitor and debug LLM routing decisions

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug

Each router has its own page with five tabs. This guide covers what each is for, and how to read a
single routing decision.

## The tabs

| Tab | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| **Activity** | See individual requests, plus spend, savings, latency, and model mix. Filter by time range, model, and call kind. |
| **Metrics** | Watch the router over time, with charts refreshed every 15 seconds. |
| **Sessions** | Replay agent sessions, with calls grouped by session. |
| **Connect** | Copy code for calling the router. See [connect an app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect). |
| **Configuration** | See and edit the router's settings: the default model, the models in the catalog, pricing, the confidence threshold, and stored provider keys. |

## Activity

The top of the page summarizes the selected time range:

| Tile | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Requests** | How many requests the router handled. |
| **Spend** | What those requests actually cost. |
| **Baseline** | What the same requests would have cost on the router's default model. |
| **Saved** | Baseline minus spend, with the percentage. |
| **Avg latency** | Mean end-to-end latency. |
| **Cache hit** | Share of prompt tokens read from cache. |

Below the tiles, **Requests over time** and **Model mix** show how traffic and cost split across
models, and a **Requests** table lists each call with its model, routing reason, tokens in and out,
cache read, cost, saving, latency, and status.

## Read a routing decision

Click any request to open its **Request detail**. It answers "why did this go there?" without
guessing.

### Decision

The model that served the request, and the **routing reason** that explains the choice. It also shows
the provider model ID, the **effort** the model was run at, and the provider.

### Classifier probabilities

The router's classifier has **one head per model and effort**: the probability that the model
passes this request at that effort. A model is confident when any effort clears the threshold, and
it's served at the lowest effort that does. The highlighted head is the one the router read.

The list covers **every model the router scores**, not only the ones in your catalog. That's how you
spot models you haven't enabled that would have been confident. See
[migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).

### Estimated cost per candidate

The expected cost of this request on each model in your catalog, which is what the router ranks the
confident models by. See [how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

### Token usage and savings

Input, output, cache read, and cache write tokens, with the request's **cost**, its **baseline**
against the default model, and the amount **saved**.

### Execution trace

How long each stage took: `ingress`, `view`, `classify`, `decide`, `serve`, and `complete`. It
separates the routing decision, which is `classify` and `decide`, from the time the provider took to
`serve` the request.

### Input and output

If the router stores session replay, the detail also shows the request's input and the model's
output. With zero data retention on, the router doesn't keep them. See
[Sessions and replay](#sessions-and-replay).

## Routing reasons

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `cheapest_confident` | At least one model was confident, and the cheapest of them served the request. |
| `default_no_confident` | No model cleared the confidence threshold, so the request went to the default model. |
| Escalation | The default wasn't confident, and the only confident model was more expensive, so the request went to that model. |

For how these come out of the decision, see
[how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

## Metrics

**Metrics** charts the router over time. Choose 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours, or 7 days, and the charts
refresh every 15 seconds:

- **Requests**, split into succeeded and errors.
- **Spend vs. the all-default baseline.**
- **Routing mix**: each model's share of calls.
- **Tokens**: fresh input, cached read, and output.
- **Cache hit rate**: cached read as a share of prompt tokens.
- **Mean latency.**

The baseline prices each request against the default model that was configured when it was served,
so it stays honest if you change the default later.

## Sessions and replay

**Sessions** groups calls by the agent session id. A session appears once an agent sends a session
header, which Claude Code does automatically. Rows without a session id aren't replayable, but
still appear in Activity.

Replay needs stored session data. If **zero data retention** is on, Emissary doesn't keep input,
output, or session replay data. It stores only routing decisions, token counts and cost telemetry.
The router list shows each router's setting under **Data retention**.

## Diagnose common situations

| You see | Likely cause | What to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Most requests go to the default model, with `default_no_confident` | The threshold is high for your catalog, or no model in it covers this traffic | Lower the [threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold), or add a model that fits the traffic |
| Requests are escalating to expensive models often | The default model is a weak one, so pricier models keep stepping in | Pick a stronger [default model](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models#choose-a-default-model) |
| A cheap model never serves | Its probability is below the threshold on your traffic | Check its head in **Classifier probabilities** before lowering the threshold |
| An image request went somewhere unexpected | The catalog may not include many vision-capable models | Check the **Vision** column on the Configuration tab |
| Cost isn't what you expected | The router ranks on the prices it has | Check your [pricing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing), and **Estimated cost per candidate** |
| Savings look low | The traffic is hard, or the catalog's cheaper models aren't covering it | Compare **Model mix** with the baseline, and see [what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights) |

For what the aggregate picture can tell you about your workload, see
[what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights).


---

# What emerges from LLM routing

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights

The obvious reasons to route are cost, performance, and latency. The less obvious ones emerge from
routing itself. A router classifies every request against every model and keeps the result. That
gives you two things a single-model setup can't:

1. **Intelligence about your workload**: what's easy, what's hard, and what you're missing.
2. **A path to your own models**: dedicated inference for the open models you route to, and
   post-training on the trajectories your traffic leaves behind.

## What does routing tell you about your workload?
### What's recorded for every request

For each request, the router records:

- **Each model's confidence** that it could complete the request.
- **The routing reason**: why a particular model was chosen, including whether the request fell to
  the default because nothing was confident, or escalated because the only confident model was more
  expensive.

You see both by clicking into a request in **Activity**. The detail also shows an estimated cost
per candidate, the saving against the baseline, and an execution trace. See
[monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).

### Which models you're missing

The router predicts confidence across all models, including ones you haven't enabled, and lists
them all under **Classifier probabilities** in each request's detail. If a model
outside your catalog is confident on a large share of your traffic, that's a candidate to add,
whether for cost, speed, or quality. See [migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).

### Which requests nothing can handle

Requests that end in `default_no_confident` are the ones **no model in your catalog could vouch
for**. Looking at what they have in common tells you where your capability gaps are:

- If they're a coherent type of task, that's a candidate for a **stronger model**, or for a model
  of your own, trained on that task. See
  [from routing to your own models](#from-routing-to-your-own-models).
- If they're scattered, your threshold may be set too high, and the router is being cautious on
  requests that a lower threshold would handle.

### Where your default model is doing the work

A high share of traffic on the default model tells you the catalog's cheaper models aren't
covering enough, or that the default is carrying work a cheaper model could do. Frequent
**escalation** says the opposite: the default is too weak for the traffic it receives.

### How difficult your traffic really is

Spread across models, with confidence, shows what share of your workload is easy and what share
needs a frontier model. Teams often guess at this, and the routing record measures it.

## How does routing lead to your own models?
Routing is the first step of a loop: **route, serve, post-train.** Each step makes the next one
possible, and the last makes routing cheaper again.

```
        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                                           │
     route ──▶ serve open models ──▶ post-train on trajectories ────┘
   (decide)    (dedicated capacity)   (your model joins the catalog)
```

### Dedicated inference

Routing sends a lot of work to open models, and **shared endpoints price those models for the
average workload, not yours.** Dedicated inference runs them on compute that's tuned to your
traffic shape, so the cheap option stays cheap and predictable:

- **Dedicated capacity**, with no noisy neighbors.
- **Tuned to your traffic shape**, rather than to an average.
- **Predictable latency under load.**

The router shows you which models carry your traffic, which tells you what to put on dedicated
capacity. See [inference](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/concept) and [deployments](https://docs.withemissary.com/inference/deployments).

### Post-training

Every routed request leaves a **trajectory**. Post-training turns those trajectories into a model of
your own, specialized to the work you actually do:

- **Cheaper** on work you've already seen.
- **Better on your domain** than any general model.
- **Faster**, because it's smaller.

When a model you trained becomes the better call for a request, the router sends it there
automatically. It's just another model in the catalog, scored for confidence like the rest. See
[post-training concepts](https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/concept).

Your data trains your models, and your signal never trains anyone else's.

Training uses the trajectories your traffic leaves behind, so it needs that data to be kept. With
**zero data retention** on, which is the default, Emissary doesn't retain input, output, or session
replay data. See [monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug#sessions-and-replay).

### The loop

**Routing feeds your training data, and training makes routing cheaper.** The more you route, the
more trajectories you have to learn from. The routing record shows which requests nothing handles
confidently, which are the best candidates for a model of your own. And the router decides, request
by request, when that model is the better call.

## Why is this useful?
Most model decisions are made on public benchmarks and intuition. Routing data comes from *your*
requests, so it answers questions specific to your workload: which model should I add, where is my
catalog weak, what should I serve on dedicated capacity, and what should I train next.


---

# Model routing FAQ: LLM router questions

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/faq

## Basics

### What is model routing?

Model routing is choosing, for each request, which model should handle it. A model router sits in
front of a pool of models, reads each request, and sends it to the model best suited to the job.
See [what is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing).

### What is an LLM router?

An LLM router is another name for a model router: software that decides which large language model
serves each request, so easy requests stop paying for a frontier model. See
[what is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing).

### How does Emissary's router decide which model to use?

It estimates each model's confidence that it can complete the request, keeps the models at or above
your confidence threshold, and picks the cheapest of them. If none is confident, the request goes to
your default model. See [how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

### Does Emissary work with the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs?

Yes. Every router is reached through one gateway URL that is compatible with the OpenAI and
Anthropic APIs. To switch an existing integration, change the base URL and the `model` string. See
[connect an app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect).

### Can I route Claude Code or other coding agents?

Yes. Point the agent at the gateway and every request it makes is routed. See
[connect an app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect#coding-agents).

### Does Emissary retain my prompts and responses?

Not by default. Zero data retention is on by default, so Emissary doesn't retain input, output or
session replay data from gateway traffic, only routing decisions, token counts and cost telemetry.
Turning it off lets you replay sessions and is the raw material for
[what emerges from routing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/insights). See [get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started).

## Concepts

### What's the difference between a router and a gateway?

A gateway handles *how* requests reach models, and a router decides *which model* serves each one.
Emissary can be both: one gateway URL with a router behind it, which we recommend, or the routing
policy alongside a gateway you already run. See
[routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways).

### What's the difference between complexity-based and performance-based routing?

Complexity-based routing guesses how hard a task is from its input and picks a cheap or expensive
model, and that's hard to do reliably. Performance-based routing, which is what Emissary does, asks
which models can actually do the task, based on how they've performed. See
[the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space#what-the-router-optimizes-for).

### Does the router choose effort, or only the model?

Both. Changing a model's effort keeps you on the same model, so the prompt cache is preserved,
while switching models loses it. See
[what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#effort).

### Can the router handle images?

The router knows which models accept images and won't send an image request to a text-only model.
It doesn't interpret the image content itself. See
[what the router sees](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/what-the-router-sees#modality).

### What's the relationship to the older router quickstart?

The earlier [router quickstart](https://docs.withemissary.com/quickstart/router) describes the stateless router. The routers
documented in this section are stateful, model-aware, and rank on cache state, output length and
effort.

## Quality, cost and latency

### Does routing reduce quality?

It shouldn't, and it can improve it. Models are strong at different things, so routing each request
to the model that handles it best can outperform any single model on your workload as a whole. The
router first keeps models it's confident can do the task, and only then ranks them by cost. See
[how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).

### How much will I save?

It depends on your traffic. A workload where most requests need a frontier model saves less than
one with many routine requests. Cache and effort decisions add savings for agentic workloads.
Measure on a sample of your own traffic. See [run a trial](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial).

### Does the router add latency?

A routing decision takes some time, so a router adds a small amount to each request. Requests that
go to a faster model finish sooner. Measure end-to-end latency on your workload rather than the
routing step alone.

## Using Emissary

### Which models can I route between?

The models in your router's catalog, which you choose when you create it. See
[choose your models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models).

### Can I create a router through the API?

Not yet. Routers are created and configured in the dashboard. Once created, you call a router
through the gateway API. See [get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started).

### How do I know why a request went to a particular model?

Click into the request in Activity. You'll see each model's confidence and the routing reason. See
[monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).

### What happens when a new model is released?

The router already scores models you haven't enabled, so you can see whether it could take a
meaningful share of your traffic. Enabling it needs no application changes. See
[migrate to new models](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/migrate-to-new-models).

## Choosing

### When shouldn't I use a router?

When you can select models offline, for example a workflow with fixed steps. See
[when to route, and when not to](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#when-to-route-and-when-not-to).

### How do I choose a router?

Use the [router selection checklist](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/selection-checklist). It covers fit, decision quality,
state and cost, modality, integration and evidence. To compare specific products, see
[compare LLM routers](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison).


---

# LLM router comparison: OpenRouter, LiteLLM and more

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison

**Short answer:** pick a **router** when you want the model chosen for you, request by request, from
evidence about what each model can do. Pick a **gateway** when your main need is model coverage,
self-hosting, or one key and one bill. Emissary is a router that also works as a gateway. This page
puts it next to four other options. Each has its own detailed page, linked below.

*Based on public information as of October 2026. Check each vendor's site for current details.*

## How do Emissary, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Not Diamond and Router.com compare?

| | **Emissary** | **OpenRouter** | **LiteLLM** | **Not Diamond** | **Router.com** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Category** | Router, with a gateway | Unified API and marketplace with provider routing | Open-source gateway and proxy, with a routing layer | Model routing company: an API router, and a local proxy for coding agents | Ramp's LLM routing layer: a gateway with pluggable routing policies |
| **How the model is chosen** | A router trained on rollouts predicts, per model and effort, whether it can complete the task, then picks the cheapest confident one, taking cache state, output length and effort into account | You choose the model, and it routes across providers. An auto-router option (`openrouter/auto`) picks among models | You write rules and config: model groups, weights, fallbacks | The API router recommends a model. Not Diamond Code routes from derived metadata such as a complexity classification | Its own cheapest-approved-model-above-a-quality-bar strategy, or another policy you plug in |
| **Who executes the call** | Emissary's gateway, on your provider keys | OpenRouter, billed through credits | The proxy you host | Your application, for the API router. A local proxy, for Not Diamond Code | Router.com, as one endpoint across providers |
| **Strength** | Routing decisions grounded in model capability and cost, with tracked savings | Breadth of models behind one key and one bill | Near-complete model coverage, and self-hosting | Routing from metadata alone, without request content | Finance integration and spend controls |

## Which LLM router should I choose?

- **You want the model chosen automatically for each request,** with quality protected by a
  confidence threshold: [Emissary](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision).
- **You want the broadest model coverage in a self-hosted gateway,** and your routing is simple
  enough to manage as rules: [LiteLLM](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-litellm).
- **You want a wide catalog behind one API key and one bill,** and your main need is availability
  and price across providers for models you've already chosen: [OpenRouter](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-openrouter).
- **You want routing that works only from metadata,** or a local proxy for a coding agent:
  [Not Diamond](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-notdiamond).
- **Finance integration is the priority,** with inference spend flowing into Ramp's reporting:
  [Router.com](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-router-com).

## What does "routing" mean across these products?

The word covers different jobs. **Provider routing** chooses which provider serves a model you
already picked. **Reliability routing** is load balancing, retries and fallbacks. **Model routing**
chooses which *model* should serve each request. Most gateways do the first two and some offer a
version of the third. See [routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways) and
[the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space).

## How should I evaluate any router?

Whichever products you shortlist, test on your own requests rather than on a vendor's figures. Use
the [router selection checklist](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/selection-checklist) to decide what matters for your workload,
and [run a trial on your traffic](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial) to measure cost, latency and quality against your
current setup.

## Detailed comparisons

- [Emissary vs OpenRouter](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-openrouter)
- [Emissary vs LiteLLM](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-litellm)
- [Emissary vs Not Diamond](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-notdiamond)
- [Emissary vs Router.com](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-router-com)

# Emissary vs OpenRouter: model vs provider routing

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-openrouter

[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) is a unified API over many models and providers. Its routing
features are mostly **provider routing**: for a model you choose, it load balances across the
providers serving it, with options to sort by price, throughput, or latency, to allow or ignore
specific providers, and to fall back to another. It also offers an auto-router model
(`openrouter/auto`) that picks among a set of models for a prompt, powered by Not Diamond.

OpenRouter is best thought of as a **marketplace and gateway**, with a routing option on top.

*Based on public information as of October 2026. Check each vendor's site for current details.*

## How does Emissary compare with OpenRouter?
| | **Emissary** | **OpenRouter** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Category** | Router and gateway | Unified API / marketplace with provider routing |
| **Main routing axis** | *Which model* can do this task, at what expected cost | *Which provider* serves a model you picked, plus an auto-router option |
| **Per-request model choice** | A router trained on rollouts of your pool | Auto-router option; otherwise you choose the model |
| **Cache, output-length and effort awareness** | Part of the ranking | Not part of provider routing by default |
| **Billing** | Your own provider keys | Credits, with a fee on credit purchases |
| **Strength** | Routing decisions grounded in model capability and cost | Breadth of models behind a single key and bill |

## Two meanings of "routing"

**Provider routing** answers: "I want model X. Which of the providers hosting X should serve it?"
That's about price, throughput, latency, and availability for a fixed model.

**Model routing** answers: "Which model should handle this request at all?" That's a question
about capability and cost across *different* models, and it's what Emissary does.

They can work together. OpenRouter is one of the providers you can use inside an Emissary router:
add OpenRouter's key, and models served through it can be part of your catalog.

## When OpenRouter is a good fit

- You want access to a wide catalog of models through one API key and one bill.
- Your main need is availability and price across providers for models you've already chosen.

## When Emissary is a better fit

- You want the model itself chosen per request, with quality protected by a confidence threshold.
- Your workloads are agentic or conversational, where cache state, effort, and output length drive
  cost.
- You want to use your own provider keys and contract pricing, and to see why each request was
  routed as it was.

## See also

- [Compare LLM routers](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison): Emissary next to OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Not Diamond
  and Router.com.
- [What is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing)


---

# Emissary vs LiteLLM: router vs gateway

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-litellm

[LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai) is an open-source SDK and proxy server that exposes many model
providers behind one OpenAI-compatible interface. Its routing features are about **reliability and
traffic management**: load balancing across deployments of the same model, retries, cooldowns, and
fallbacks to another model group when a call fails.

Emissary can also be your gateway: one URL, compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, calling
providers with your own keys. The difference is what decides *which model* serves a request. With
LiteLLM, you manage that yourself, with rules and configuration you write. With Emissary, it's
automated, by a router trained to predict which models can do the task. See
[routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways).

*Based on public information as of October 2026. Check each vendor's site for current details.*

## How does Emissary compare with LiteLLM?
| | **Emissary** | **LiteLLM** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Category** | Router, with a gateway | Gateway / proxy, with a routing layer |
| **Model routing** | Automated: a router trained on rollouts predicts, per model, whether it can complete the task | Self-managed: rules and config you write, such as model groups, weights, and fallbacks |
| **Model coverage** | The models in Emissary's catalog | Almost all models |
| **Savings** | Tracked per request and in aggregate against a baseline | Cost tracking, with routing savings up to your rules |
| **Model migration** | The router scores models you haven't enabled, and you can A/B a new model | You update your config and rules |
| **Hosting** | Managed gateway at `api.withemissary.com` | Open source, self-hosted |

## When LiteLLM is a good fit

- You need the broadest **model coverage** in a gateway. LiteLLM supports almost every model.
- You want to **self-host** the gateway, with keys, retries, timeouts, and fallbacks under your own
  infrastructure.
- Your routing is simple enough to manage yourself as rules, or you only need reliability across
  deployments of the same model.

## When Emissary is a better fit

- You want **automated model routing** rather than self-managed routing: the choice of model made
  per request from evidence about what each model can do, with no rules to maintain as models and
  prices change.
- You want **actual, tracked, meaningful savings**: Activity and Metrics show spend against a
  baseline, and each request records why it went where it did.
- You want **easy model migrations**: the router tells you which new models fit your traffic, and
  you can test one on a second router before you commit.

## See also

- [Compare LLM routers](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison): Emissary next to OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Not Diamond
  and Router.com.
- [What is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing)


---

# Emissary vs Not Diamond: routing compared

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-notdiamond

[Not Diamond](https://www.notdiamond.ai) is a model routing company. Its API router recommends a
model for an input, and your application then executes the request through its own gateway, with
custom routers trained on your evaluation data. Its coding-agent product, Not Diamond Code, works
differently: it's a local proxy that routes from **derived metadata** rather than from the content
of each request.

According to its data dictionary, Not Diamond Code always collects metadata such as request and
session IDs, the requested and routed models, a **complexity classification**, the effort level,
and token counts. Request and response bodies, and local transcripts, are off by default and are
collected only if an account owner or admin enables sensitive data collection. Without consent,
routing relies on that metadata.

*Based on public information as of October 2026. Check each vendor's site for current details.*

## How does Emissary compare with Not Diamond?
| | **Emissary** | **Not Diamond Code** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Routing signal** | The request itself, scored against each model: one confidence estimate per model and effort | Derived metadata: complexity classification, effort, and usage telemetry such as token and session data |
| **Query × model prediction** | Yes: the probability that *this model* passes *this request* | No: routing doesn't predict per-request, per-model success from the content |
| **What it optimizes for** | Performance: which models can do the task, then the cheapest of them | Complexity: how hard the task looks, then a cheap or expensive model |
| **Cache, output-length and effort awareness** | Part of the ranking | Effort level is tracked |
| **Execution** | The gateway calls the chosen model, on your provider keys | A local proxy sits between your agent and the provider |

## Where the approaches differ

**What the router looks at.** Emissary's router reads the request and estimates, for each model and
effort, the probability that it completes the task. That's a prediction about a specific query and
a specific model. A metadata-based router never sees the query's content, so it can't make that
kind of prediction. It can only act on signals such as how complex the work looks and how usage is
trending.

**Complexity vs performance.** Estimating complexity from metadata is a version of
complexity-based routing, which is hard to do reliably, because complexity is hard to read from the
input. Emissary asks which models can actually do the task, based on how they've performed. See
[the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space#what-the-router-optimizes-for).

**Privacy trade-off.** Not routing on content is a real benefit if you can't send prompts, code, or
outputs to a third party. Emissary's router does read the request to score it, with
[zero data retention](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started) on by default, so Emissary doesn't keep input, output, or
session replay data unless you turn it off.

**Cost as a second step.** Emissary separates capability from cost. Models above your threshold
form the confident pool, and only then are they ranked on price, expected output length, and cache
state. That keeps cost from overriding quality.

## When Not Diamond is a good fit

- You want routing that works only from metadata, without request content.
- Your priority is a local proxy for a coding agent, and a rough complexity-based split is enough.

## When Emissary is a better fit

- You want routing based on whether a specific model can do a specific request, not on how complex
  the request looks.
- You run long conversations or agent loops where cache state matters.
- You need output length, effort, and your own contract pricing in the cost decision.
- You'd rather have one endpoint that both decides and executes.

## See also

- [Compare LLM routers](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison): Emissary next to OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Not Diamond
  and Router.com.
- [What is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing)


---

# Emissary vs Router.com: routing compared

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-router-com

[Router.com](https://router.com) is Ramp's LLM routing layer, and it's closer to a gateway than a
router. It gives you one endpoint across providers, with fallbacks, spend tracking, and per-request
inspection, and it ties inference spend into Ramp's financial reporting. Its own strategy sends each
request to the cheapest approved model that meets a quality bar, and it supports other routing
policies too, such as Jev and NemoSwitchyard.

*Based on public information as of October 2026. Check each vendor's site for current details.*

## How does Emissary compare with Router.com?
| | **Emissary** | **Router.com** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Category** | Router, with a gateway | Gateway with pluggable routing policies |
| **How the decision is made** | A router post-trained on rollouts of the models in your pool, with one confidence estimate per model and effort | Its own cheapest-approved-model-above-a-quality-bar strategy, or another routing policy you plug in |
| **Endpoint** | One gateway URL, compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs | One endpoint across providers |
| **Cache, output-length and effort awareness** | Part of the ranking | Depends on the policy |
| **Custom pricing** | Used in ranking | Not described publicly |
| **Strength** | Automated routing quality for agentic and multi-step workloads, with tracked savings | Finance integration and spend controls, and a choice of routing policies |

## When Router.com is a good fit

- Finance integration is the priority, with inference spend flowing into Ramp's reporting.
- You want a gateway that can run different routing policies, and you'd rather pick or build the
  policy yourself.
- Your main goals are cost control and provider fallbacks.

## When Emissary is a better fit

- You want **automated routing** grounded in how each model actually performs, not a static quality
  bar or a policy you have to choose and maintain.
- You run long conversations or agent loops where **cache state**, **effort**, and **output length**
  change which option is actually cheapest.
- You want routing trained on your own task distribution, priced with your own contract rates, and
  an auditable record of why each request went where it did.

See [how a routing decision is made](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/decision), and the
[selection checklist](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/selection-checklist) to evaluate any router against your needs.

## See also

- [Compare LLM routers](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/llm-router-comparison): Emissary next to OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Not Diamond
  and Router.com.
- [What is model routing?](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/what-is-model-routing)


---

# How to test an LLM router on your traffic

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial

A router's value depends on your traffic, so the only trustworthy test is on your traffic. Treat any
vendor's savings figure, including ours, as a claim until you've measured it on your own requests.

## 1. Build a representative sample

Collect a set of real requests that reflects your workload. Include the easy ones, the hard ones,
and the odd ones, because the mix is what determines routing. For agents, use whole
multi-step runs rather than isolated calls, since cache and effort effects only show up across
steps.

## 2. Set a baseline

Run the sample through your **current** setup, typically a single model, and record:

- **Cost**: total spend for the sample.
- **Latency**: end-to-end, per request or per step.
- **Quality**: however you measure it today, whether evals, graded outputs, or task success.

## 3. Create a router and run the same sample

Create a router with a [catalog](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/choose-your-models) and the default
[threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold), and send the sample through it. See
[get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started) and [connect an app or agent](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/connect).

## 4. Compare

Compare against the baseline on all three: cost, latency, and quality. Look at quality first.
Savings that come with a quality drop aren't savings.

## 5. Read the routing decisions

In **Activity**, click into requests and read the confidence and routing reason. See
[monitor and debug](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/monitor-and-debug).

- Where did requests go, and does it match your intuition about what's easy?
- How much landed on the default model with `default_no_confident`?
- Were there escalations?

## 6. Adjust and repeat

Tune the [threshold](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/confidence-threshold), the catalog, and
[pricing](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/guides/pricing), and run again. Change one thing at a time so you know what moved the
numbers.

## What a good result looks like

- Quality holds, or improves, compared with the baseline.
- Cost and latency fall, with more of the savings on the requests that were easy.
- The requests the router considered unhandled are ones you'd have expected to be hard.

If routing doesn't help, that's a useful answer too. See
[when to route, and when not to](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#when-to-route-and-when-not-to).


---

# LLM router selection checklist

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/selection-checklist

Use this checklist to evaluate any model router, including Emissary. Not every item will matter for
every workload. The point is to know which ones do before you commit. The terms are explained in
[the router design space](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/design-space).

## 1. Fit with your workload

- [ ] **Do you need a router, a gateway, or both?** Be clear whether you need a decision about
      *which model*, a way to *reach and manage* models, or both. See
      [routers and gateways](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/how-routing-works/routers-and-gateways).
- [ ] **Does your traffic vary in difficulty?** If almost every request needs the same model,
      routing won't help much.
- [ ] **Is the front door open-ended?** If your steps are fixed, select models offline instead. See
      [when to route, and when not to](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/why-route#when-to-route-and-when-not-to).
- [ ] **Are your workloads agentic or conversational?** If so, state and cache matter (see 3).

## 2. Decision quality

- [ ] **Is the router performance-based or complexity-based?** Does it estimate which models can do
      the task, or guess how hard the task is from the input?
- [ ] **Is it model-aware?** Was it trained on how the models in *your* pool actually perform, or
      does it only map query text to a label?
- [ ] **How is quality protected?** Is there a confidence threshold you control, so cost savings
      can't override quality?
- [ ] **Can you see why it routed a request?** You need that to trust and tune it.
- [ ] **How does it adapt when models change?** Adding or updating a model shouldn't mean starting
      over, and ideally it tells you which new models fit your traffic.

## 3. State and cost

- [ ] **Is it stateful?** Does it know what each model has cached, and use it?
- [ ] **Does it route across effort as well as models?** Changing effort on the same model keeps the
      cache.
- [ ] **Is it intelligence-density aware?** Does it price in expected output tokens, not just
      per-token price?
- [ ] **Does it support custom pricing?** Contract rates and discounts should be reflected in the
      ranking.

## 4. Modality

- [ ] **Is it modality-aware?** It must not route images to text-only models.
- [ ] **Do you need it to be multimodal?** Only if image content should influence the decision.

## 5. Integration and operations

- [ ] **Does it return a recommendation, or execute the call?** Which fits your stack?
- [ ] **Does it work with your SDKs and agents?** For example, OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible APIs,
      and coding agents.
- [ ] **Whose provider keys does it use?** Yours, or credits you buy from the router.
- [ ] **What does the routing step cost in latency and money?** Measure on your own workload.
- [ ] **What happens when the router is unavailable?** Is there a safe default?

## 6. Evidence

- [ ] **Run a trial on your own traffic.** See [run a trial](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/run-a-trial).
- [ ] **Treat vendor savings figures as claims**, not predictions, until you've measured them.

Ready to try Emissary? Start with [get started](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/get-started), and see how it compares in
[Emissary vs Router.com](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-router-com), [vs LiteLLM](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-litellm),
[vs Not Diamond](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-notdiamond), and [vs OpenRouter](https://docs.withemissary.com/routing/evaluate/emissary-vs-openrouter).


---

# What is post-training? SFT, GRPO and fine-tuning

Source: https://docs.withemissary.com/fine-tuning/what-is-post-training

**Post-training** is how you adapt a base model to your specific task. Prompting only changes what
you put *into* a model. Post-training changes the model's **weights**, which gives you more stable,
precise and differentiated behavior than prompt engineering can reach. On Emissary you start from a
